units.title: Unit 89 — Adjectives
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 89. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish extreme adjectives from ordinary gradable adjectives and select appropriate intensifiers.
Use absolutely and really naturally with extreme adjectives and avoid very + extreme adjective.
Understand strong positive and negative descriptions such as marvellous, dreadful, tiny, enormous and fascinating.
Differentiate -ing adjectives describing causes from -ed adjectives describing a person’s feelings.
Choose accurate feeling and situation adjectives in short exchanges and descriptions.

items.example: We had marvellous weather during our holiday.
items.note: An extreme positive adjective; absolutely or really can be used with it.

items.example: The concert was absolutely terrific.
items.note: An extreme positive adjective similar to marvellous and wonderful.

items.example: We had a wonderful time at the festival.
items.note: A very strong positive description; often used with absolutely or really.

items.example: The view from the mountain was amazing.
items.note: Describes something that causes strong surprise or admiration.

items.example: The hotel service was absolutely awful.
items.note: An extreme negative adjective, not normally very awful.

items.example: We had dreadful weather all weekend.
items.note: A very strong negative adjective similar to awful.

items.example: I was delighted to hear that you passed the exam.
items.note: Stronger than pleased; can be used with absolutely.

items.example: They live in a tiny flat near the station.
items.note: An extreme adjective meaning very small.

items.example: A huge crowd waited outside the theatre.
items.note: An extreme adjective meaning very big.

items.example: The new library has an enormous reading room.
items.note: Similar in strength and meaning to huge.

items.example: I watched a fascinating documentary about the ocean.
items.note: An extreme adjective meaning very interesting.

items.example: By the end of the hike, everyone was exhausted.
items.note: Stronger than tired; describes a person’s state.

items.example: The climb down the narrow path was terrifying.
items.note: Describes something that causes extreme fear.

items.example: The children were terrified during the storm.
items.note: Extreme -ed adjective meaning very frightened; featured in the classification exercise.

items.example: Good preparation is essential for a safe journey.
items.note: An extreme adjective meaning very important and necessary.

items.example: The soup was absolutely delicious.
items.note: Usually describes food or drink; means extremely good-tasting.

items.example: The performance was absolutely wonderful.
items.note: A frequent intensifier for extreme adjectives such as wonderful, tiny and awful.

items.example: That was a really interesting conversation.
items.note: Can intensify both gradable and extreme adjectives.

items.example: The room was very small but comfortable.
items.note: Typically intensifies gradable adjectives, not extreme adjectives.

items.example: The traffic was absolutely awful this morning.
items.note: Model collocation: absolutely + extreme adjective.

items.example: The kitchen is absolutely tiny.
items.note: Use absolutely with tiny, not with the gradable adjective small.

items.example: Our new neighbours are really terrific.
items.note: Really is also possible with extreme adjectives.

items.example: They need a very big room for the meeting.
items.note: Gradable big takes very or really, unlike extreme huge.

items.example: This screen is very small.
items.note: Gradable small contrasts with the extreme adjective tiny.

items.example: The first safety check is very important.
items.note: Gradable important contrasts with extreme essential.

items.example: I was very tired after work.
items.note: Tired is gradable; exhausted is its stronger counterpart.

items.example: He was frightened when he heard the noise.
items.note: Gradable frightened contrasts with the extreme adjective terrified.

items.example: Small is a gradable adjective, so very small is natural.
items.note: A description with degrees; very can normally be used before it.

items.pt: adjetivo extremo; adjetivo de grau máximo
items.example: Tiny is an extreme adjective meaning very small.
items.note: An adjective with a built-in strong meaning; absolutely is commonly used.

items.example: The long lecture was boring.
items.note: -ing describes something that causes boredom.

items.example: I was bored during the long lecture.
items.note: -ed describes how someone feels, not what causes that feeling.

items.example: The endless rain was depressing.
items.note: Describes a situation that causes low spirits.

items.example: He felt depressed after several disappointing days.
items.note: Describes the person’s emotional state.

items.example: Carrying all those boxes upstairs was tiring.
items.note: The activity causes tiredness; the person becomes tired.

items.example: I was amazed by how quickly the children learnt.
items.note: Describes someone experiencing strong surprise.

items.example: The results were disappointing after so much practice.
items.note: Something falls short of expectations.

items.example: We were disappointed with the small room.
items.note: A person experiences disappointment; supported by the feelings exercise.

items.example: I was annoyed when the delivery arrived late.
items.note: Describes how a person feels about an irritating event.

items.example: The constant noise was annoying.
items.note: Describes something that causes annoyance; counterpart to annoyed.

items.example: I felt embarrassed when I forgot her name.
items.note: Describes an uncomfortable feeling after a social mistake.

items.example: Forgetting his name was an embarrassing mistake.
items.note: The cause of embarrassment; counterpart to embarrassed.

items.example: The instructions were confusing.
items.note: Describes information or a situation that makes people feel confused.

items.example: The different directions left us confused.
items.note: Describes how someone feels when they do not understand.

items.pt: chocado; muito surpreso de forma desagradável
items.example: We were shocked by the unexpected news.
items.note: A strong unpleasant reaction to something surprising.

items.example: The report contained some shocking details.
items.note: Describes something that causes shock; counterpart to shocked.

items.example: They are interested in the new exhibition.
items.note: A person feels interest: be interested in something, not be interesting in it.

items.example: The talk about local history was interesting.
items.note: A thing or activity attracts interest; do not confuse with interested.

items.example: I was surprised to see the room so tidy.
items.note: The person experiences surprise; illustrated by the feelings exercise.

items.example: It was surprising to see everyone arrive so early.
items.note: The event causes surprise; illustrated by an exercise dialogue.

items.example: The overnight journey was absolutely exhausting.
items.note: Describes an experience that causes exhaustion; used in the email rewrite.

items.example: They were disappointed with their accommodation.
items.note: A natural adjective + preposition pattern; applied to the holiday exercise.

sectionsChecked: A: Extreme adjectives, synonyms and intensifier language help
B: -ing and -ed adjective pairs and common mistakes
Exercises 89.1–89.4 including email and dialogue tasks

units.title: Unit 90 — Prepositions: place and movement
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 90. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Choose at, on or in for locations, surfaces, enclosed spaces, addresses and cities.
Describe precise relative positions with beyond, beside, by, above, below, against, underneath and among.
Explain movement using into, out of, towards, down, up, over, under, through, round, after and past.
Distinguish contrasting preposition pairs such as before/after, above/below and into/out of.
Apply the prepositions in natural place descriptions, routes, everyday travel and common error corrections.

items.pt: em; no; na (ponto ou local específico)
items.example: I met my friend at the station.
items.note: Use at for a point or specific place, including bus stops and airports.

items.example: We waited at the bus stop in the rain.
items.note: At identifies a particular point or meeting place.

items.example: My sister is at work until six.
items.note: A common fixed location expression.

items.example: I met the visitors at the airport.
items.note: The book highlights at the airport, not on the airport.

items.example: They first met at a party.
items.note: Use at when referring to an event or gathering.

items.example: The repair shop is at number twenty-three.
items.note: At specifies a street number or precise address.

items.example: I left my exercise book at school.
items.note: At school is a common location expression.

items.example: There is a notebook on the table.
items.note: Use on for contact with a surface.

items.example: My phone is on the desk beside the laptop.
items.note: On, not in, is used for an object resting on a desk.

items.example: Please do not leave your shoes on the floor.
items.note: The floor is treated as a surface.

items.example: There is a small picture on the wall.
items.note: For pictures and objects attached to a wall, use on.

items.example: There was frost on the ground that morning.
items.note: On is used for something covering or resting on the ground.

items.example: She sat on the bed to put on her shoes.
items.note: The bed is treated as a supporting surface.

items.example: Drivers should slow down on icy roads.
items.note: Use on when describing travelling along a road; reinforced by the personal exercise.

items.pt: dentro de; em (área, espaço ou lugar)
items.example: We had lunch in the kitchen.
items.note: Use in for an enclosed area, city, country or something with an inside.

items.example: The children are in the kitchen.
items.note: Inside a room is commonly in.

items.example: The scissors are in the top drawer.
items.note: In describes something inside a drawer.

items.example: My uncle lives in London.
items.note: Use in with towns, cities and countries, unlike at + a street number.

items.example: They live in a quiet street near the park.
items.note: The book uses in Danvers Street for a street name; a common British usage.

items.example: I found the ticket in my pocket.
items.note: Use in for an object inside a pocket.

items.example: The milk is in the fridge.
items.note: In is used for an enclosed storage space.

items.pt: no jardim dos fundos; no quintal dos fundos
items.example: I found the bicycle in the back garden.
items.note: An area or space can take in, as in in the garden.

items.pt: além de; do outro lado de
items.example: Their house is beyond the old bridge.
items.note: Beyond describes a place on the far side of another reference point.

items.example: There is a cafe by the church.
items.note: Here by means near, unlike its use for an agent or means.

items.example: She sat beside her brother.
items.note: Beside means next to, often immediately adjacent.

items.pt: bem ao lado de; imediatamente junto a
items.example: They found a cottage right beside the river.
items.note: Right adds emphasis: exactly or immediately beside.

items.example: The bus station is next to the library.
items.note: Another expression for beside; explained in the presentation gloss.

items.pt: acima de; em posição superior a
items.example: Our office is above a small shop.
items.note: Describes a higher position without necessarily touching.

items.pt: abaixo de; em posição inferior a
items.example: The reception area is below our office.
items.note: The opposite of above.

items.pt: antes de (em uma sequência de lugares)
items.example: There is a petrol station before the roundabout.
items.note: In route descriptions, you reach the first place before the second.

items.pt: depois de (em uma sequência de lugares)
items.example: Turn left after the bank.
items.note: In place descriptions, after contrasts with before.

items.example: He put the bicycle against the wall.
items.note: Describes physical contact with a surface; not merely near.

items.example: The old photograph was beneath a pile of papers.
items.note: Similar to under; slightly more formal in some contexts.

items.example: Her keys were underneath the cushions.
items.note: Means directly under another object.

items.example: The bag is under the chair.
items.note: Common counterpart to over and above; also used for a route under a structure.

items.example: We spotted a red flower among the trees.
items.note: Used when something is in a group or surrounded by several things.

items.example: The pharmacy is on the left, just before the bank.
items.note: On the left locates something along a street or route.

items.pt: perto da janela; junto à janela
items.example: I prefer to sit by the window on a train.
items.note: By means close to; practiced in the personal questions.

items.pt: para fora de; saindo de dentro de
items.example: The dog ran out of the garden.
items.note: Movement from inside to outside; the opposite of into.

items.example: The children went into the classroom.
items.note: Movement from outside to inside; contrasts with in (location).

items.example: The girl walked towards the bus stop.
items.note: Describes direction, not necessarily arriving at the destination.

items.example: We cycled down the hill.
items.note: Movement downward; the opposite of up.

items.example: They climbed up the stairs.
items.note: Movement upward; contrasted with down.

items.pt: por cima de; atravessando por cima de
items.example: The train went over the bridge.
items.note: Movement across the upper side of a structure; contrasted with under.

items.example: We walked under the bridge on our way home.
items.note: Used for movement below a structure; the opposite route to over the bridge.

items.example: The car passed through the tunnel.
items.note: Moving inside and across an enclosed or bounded space.

items.example: We walked round the lake before lunch.
items.note: British English round describes following a curved path or going around something.

items.pt: atrás de alguém; em perseguição a alguém
items.example: The woman ran after the children.
items.note: In a movement narrative, go or run after someone means follow or pursue them.

items.example: The cyclist rode past the museum.
items.note: Moving beyond a place without stopping there.

items.example: She got out of the car near the hotel.
items.note: Movement from inside a vehicle to outside; contrasts with get into a car.

items.example: He got into the car and closed the door.
items.note: Use get into for entering a car; the opposite is get out of.

items.pt: passar por cima de uma cerca; escalar uma cerca
items.example: The boy climbed over the fence.
items.note: Cross the top of an obstacle; the exercise contrasts over and under.

items.pt: passar por baixo de uma cerca
items.example: The small dog went under the fence.
items.note: Pass below an obstacle rather than over it.
